panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Panel A clinical photo from disseminated fusariosis article with caption describing erythematous-violaceous macula; culture proved Fusarium spp. from skin lesion, supporting attribution. B: Panel B shows evolution to ulceration with necrotic black center and erythematous halo, classic for disseminated fusariosis; same patient with culture-proven Fusarium spp.
panels.attribution_text: Chagas et al. Disseminated fusariosis in a patient with bone marrow aplasia.. Anais brasileiros de dermatologia 2020. doi:10.1016/j.abd.2019.12.008. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: A, An erythematous-violaceous macula on the left upper limb. B, After one week, the lesion evolved to ulceration with a necrotic center and slight erythema around it.
in_text_mentions: After the seventh day of hospitalization, the patient presented a painful, erythematous-violet macula in the left upper limb, which after one week evolved with central necrosis (Fig. 1). A lesion biopsy was performed; the histopathology was compatible with leukocytoclastic vasculitis and numerous hyphae were seen on the vessel wall (Fig. 2). Direct examination of material from the skin lesion revealed filamentous fungi. Culture in Sabouraud’s medium with chloramphenicol from the skin fragment and subsequent microculture of the colony evidenced the growth of Fusarium spp. (Figure 3, Figure 4).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Clinical photo of scrotal blister-like rash with scabs/crater-like change in article titled Disseminated fusarium infection after allo-HSCT; classic early necrotic papular evolution of disseminated fusariosis. B: Clinical photo of scattered red nodules at +9 days; in-text describes multiple 1cm tough nodules with redness; classic disseminated papulonodular lesions of disseminated fusariosis. C: Clinical photo shows two erythematous-violaceous halo lesions with central necrosis/pus; matches progressive ecthyma-like targetoid lesions of disseminated fusariosis. D: Clinical photo of face/nose shows black necrotic lesions; caption explicitly describes black necrotic healing-stage lesions of disseminated fusariosis.

panels.figure_caption: (A) At the beginning of the disease, typical blister-like rash was seen in the scrotum; which gradually developed scabs, forming crater-like changes. (B) Nine days after onset, the skin showed scattered red nodules. (C) During the progressive stage of lesions, pus formed in the center of the rashes and the lesions gradually crusted and became necrotic. (D) During the skin lesion healing period, the rashes gradually became black and necrotic.

panels.rationale: Single PAS-stained punch biopsy from right lower extremity ulcer in article titled Cutaneous Fusariosis in a Patient with Job's Syndrome; caption and in-text describe numerous fungal hyphae consistent with deep fungal infection, supporting disseminated_fusariosis histology finding.

panels.figure_caption: Punch excision skin biopsy obtained from a right lower extremity ulcer. Digestive PAS stain demonstrating the presence of numerous fungal hyphae consistent with fungal infection. Gram stain appeared negative for bacterial organisms.
in_text_mentions: A punch biopsy of the right knee lesion was performed during the initial encounter and showed an ulcer and abscess in the upper and mid-dermis. The deep dermis also exhibited suppurative inflammation within the subcutaneous tissue. Most remarkably, digestive PAS stain revealed the presence of numerous fungal hyphae consistent with deep fungal infection (Figure 3). Gram stain appeared negative for bacterial organisms.
